findings.text: In the first three paragraphs a newcomer learns what Athena is, what a study is, and that this page is a study of another project called firstmate. That covers 'what is this' well.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository." … "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: What to do next is clear. A jump link at the top leads to a short list: install Athena, read firstmate, or check a claim.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the section "Next steps"

findings.text: The page's own address is the Athena site, but almost all of it is about firstmate. Athena's case for why it matters is one sentence. The page also never shows the cost recording or the two-model check that this sentence promises, so a newcomer has to take those on trust.
findings.source: Header lede: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: Firstmate is explained in plain terms, and the reader is told why it is useful: tasks run side by side without workers overwriting each other's files. The "Words used first" list defines captain, yolo, green and red before the page uses them, which helps a lot.
findings.source: "What firstmate is": "Firstmate is a tool for people who direct AI coding agents. It keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a worker…"

findings.text: Some terms are used but never defined: "wake", "endpoint", "crew-state", "crewmates". The definition of stale wake uses the word wake without saying what a wake is.
findings.source: Glossary: "stale wake — A wake after which the agent inspects a worker…"; claim c10: "the crew-state, PR-check and secondmate publisher call the same gate"; claim c3: "creates an endpoint"

findings.text: The glossary entries for ship and secondmate mostly say what they are not. Neither says what a secondmate is for, so a newcomer cannot tell why anyone would create one.
findings.source: Glossary: "ship — A kind of task, named next to scouts."; "secondmate — A persistent firstmate home, not a worker and not a backlog item."

findings.text: The page promises three parts, but four subsections follow, starting with "Words used first". Also, the Transitions, Counters and Claims sections are dense reference material (t1–t11, c1–c44) that a newcomer will probably skim. That is acceptable only because the plain summary comes first.
findings.source: "Start here": "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails…"

findings.text: The findings are numbered f1, f3, f4, with no f2 and no explanation, so a reader may think something is missing. The section is still useful: it says honestly that nothing in firstmate was run and every claim comes only from reading the source.
findings.source: "Limits of this study": items f1, f3, f4

findings.text: The glossary calls both done and reopened "the final state", which is confusing. The States section handles this more clearly by saying both carry the tag "ends the task".
findings.source: Glossary: "done — The final state…" and "reopened — The final state of a task…"
